The '''English football champions''' are the annual winners of the top-tier competition in the [[English football league system]]. Following the codification of [[Professionalism in association football|professional football]] by [[the Football Association]] in 1885,<ref>{{cite web |title=The History of the Football League |publisher=The Football League |url=http://www.football-league.premiumtv.co.uk/page/History/0,,10794,00.html |access-date=15 February 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070211234251/http://www.football-league.premiumtv.co.uk/page/History/0%2C%2C10794%2C00.html |archive-date=11 February 2007}}</ref> the [[English Football League|Football League]] was established in 1888, after meetings initiated by [[Aston Villa F.C.|Aston Villa]] director [[William McGregor (football)|William McGregor]].{{sfn|Inglis|1988|pp=6–8}}

The new league's inaugural season was [[1888–89 in English football|1888–89]], and the first club to be crowned champions was [[Preston North End F.C.|Preston North End]], whose team completed its fixtures unbeaten.<ref name="WSC">{{cite web |last=Titford |first=Roger |url=http://www.wsc.co.uk/content/view/1498/29/ |title=Football League, 1888–89 |work=When Saturday Comes |date=November 2005 |access-date=6 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090529002229/http://www.wsc.co.uk/content/view/1498/29/ |archive-date=29 May 2009 |url-status=dead}}</ref> In its first four seasons, with only twelve to fourteen clubs involved, the league was a single entity in which all the teams were from the [[North of England|North]] or the [[Midlands]]. Professionalism had been embraced more readily in those areas than in the [[South of England]].<ref name="Goldblatt">{{cite book |last=Goldblatt |first=David |title=The Ball is Round: A Global History of Football |publisher=Penguin |location=London |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-14-101582-8 |page=58}}</ref> The Football League expanded its membership in 1892 when it absorbed the rival [[Football Alliance]]. With 28 members, the league was split into two divisions. Most of the former Alliance clubs joined the new [[Football League Second Division|Second Division]], while the original league became the [[Football League First Division|First Division]], with [[promotion and relegation]] between the two.{{sfn|Inglis|1988|p=25}}

Rules stipulating a maximum wage for players were abolished in 1961. This resulted in a shift of power towards bigger clubs with more financial means.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/burnley-little-town-big-traditions-206qtm2zrsq |title=Burnley: little town, big traditions |newspaper=The Times |access-date=18 January 2025 |location=London |first=Tom |last=Dart |date=25 May 2009}}</ref> Financial considerations became an even bigger influence from 1992, when the clubs then in the First Division [[Foundation of the Premier League|defected]] to form the [[Premier League|FA Premier League]], which became the new top tier.<ref name="premsitehistory">{{cite web |url=http://www.premierleague.com/page/History/0,,12306,00.html |title=A History of The Premier League |publisher=Premier League |access-date=7 June 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111118121453/http://www.premierleague.com/page/History/0%2C%2C12306%2C00.html |archive-date=18 November 2011}}</ref> A series of progressively larger television contracts has put unprecedented wealth into the hands of top flight clubs.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/premier-league/163178bn-record-premier-league-tv-deal-defies-economic-slump-1569576.html |title=£1.78bn: Record Premier League TV deal defies economic slump |newspaper=The Independent |access-date=15 June 2009 |location=London |first=Nick |last=Harris |date=7 February 2009 |archive-date=28 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170828193023/http://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/premier-league/163178bn-record-premier-league-tv-deal-defies-economic-slump-1569576.html |url-status=live}}</ref>

==List of champion clubs by titles won==
24 clubs have won the English top level title, including seven which have won the Premier League (1992–present). The most recent to join the list were [[Leicester City F.C.|Leicester City]] (2015–16) and before that, [[Nottingham Forest F.C.|Nottingham Forest]] (1977–78) and [[Derby County F.C.|Derby County]] (1971–72).

Seven teams have at some point held first or joint first place in the number of titles won: [[Preston North End F.C.|Preston North End]] (1889–1895), [[Sunderland A.F.C.|Sunderland]] (1893–1899, 1936–1953), [[Aston Villa F.C.|Aston Villa]] (1897–1953), [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] (1948–1976), [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] (1966–1971, 1973–2011, 2025–present), [[Manchester United F.C.|Manchester United]] (1967–1971, 2009–present), and [[Everton F.C.|Everton]] (1970–1971).

Eight teams have finished as runners-up without ever finishing top: [[Bristol City F.C.|Bristol City]] (1906–07), [[Oldham Athletic A.F.C.|Oldham Athletic]] (1914–15), [[Cardiff City F.C.|Cardiff City]] (1923–24), [[Charlton Athletic F.C.|Charlton Athletic]] (1936–37), [[Blackpool F.C.|Blackpool]] (1955–56), [[Queens Park Rangers F.C.|Queens Park Rangers]] (1975–76), [[Watford F.C.|Watford]] (1982–83), and [[Southampton F.C.|Southampton]] (1983–84). Of these, Cardiff City came closest to winning the league, matching champions [[Huddersfield Town A.F.C.|Huddersfield Town]] in points but losing out on [[goal average]] (goals scored divided by goals conceded), the precursor to [[goal difference]].

Where teams in the table are tied for championship wins, they are ordered by earliest title won.
